own_scenes.desc: La edad de oro sacó el hip hop de la fiesta hacia la política: «A.F.R.I.C.A.» de Stetsasonic (1987), con la Africa Fund y hasta una guía de estudio, fue de los primeros temas afrocéntricos. Grupos como X Clan (el Blackwatch Movement de Paradise Gray), Poor Righteous Teachers y Brand Nubian difundían las enseñanzas de la Nación del Islam y de los Five Percenters: el conocimiento pasó a respetarse tanto como la lírica. Les acusaban de odiar a los blancos; respondían que había que salvar primero a los suyos del crack y de las leyes de los tres strikes. Cuando la prensa culpó al rap de la violencia (Run-DMC en Long Beach en 1986, el apuñalamiento del Dope Jam en el Nassau Coliseum en 1988, que prohibió el rap), KRS-One, Ann Carli y Nelson George reunieron a Public Enemy, Kool Moe Dee, Just-Ice, MC Lyte o Stetsasonic en «Self Destruction» (1989): casi tres meses número 1 y más de cien mil dólares para la National Urban League.

refs.q: So that was a big part of it, that knowledge became as respected in hip-hop as lyricism, as DJing, as rapping.
refs.para: And also, we started representing a lot of the teachings of the Nation of Islam with groups like the Poor Righteous Teachers, and Big Daddy Kane, and KRS-One. Brand Nubian were espousing the science of the Five Percenters. So that was a big part of it, that knowledge became as respected in hip-hop as lyricism, as DJing, as rapping.

refs.q: We didn’t make crack. Crack was put in the community, and now we’re penalized for it and it’s hurting a lot of our people.
refs.para: And we were like, “We’ve got this crack epidemic going on that’s taking a large percentage of our population. We’ve got this new law about drug selling that’s a three-strike law that’s sending a lot of our brothers to jail. We didn’t make crack. Crack was put in the community, and now we’re penalized for it and it’s hurting a lot of our people. We’ve got to stop this.”
